meters.label: Segments the sender may have in flight
Segments waiting in the router queue

frames.narration: A client downloads a 5 MB file (3,425 segments of 1,460 bytes) over a 100 Mbit/s link with an 80 ms RTT. To fill that link the server needs bandwidth x RTT = 1 MB, about 684 segments, in flight. It does not know that yet, so it starts with an initial window of 10.

Each ACK grows cwnd by one segment, so cwnd doubles every round trip: 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640. Six round trips in (480 ms) the sender is at 640 segments, close to the 684 the link can hold, with no loss and no queue.

Round 8 sends cwnd 1,280 into a pipe that holds 684. The extra 596 segments sit in the router buffer (1 BDP = 684 segments), so the RTT grows from 80 to 149 ms. Throughput is pinned at 100 Mbit/s; the extra window only adds delay.

The last 875 segments go out in round 9 and the transfer ends after 9 rounds and 811 ms. It never left slow start and averaged 49 Mbit/s on a 100 Mbit/s link. Short transfers are decided by the round-trip count, not by the bandwidth.

Now add 0.1% random loss. One segment of the last flight is dropped. The receiver keeps ACKing the same sequence number, and 3 duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit. cwnd is halved (ssthresh = 1,280), not reset. The repair costs one more round trip: 10 rounds, 891 ms.

At 1% loss Reno cannot grow. Each loss halves cwnd (80, 40, 20, ...) and congestion avoidance adds only 1 segment per round, so the window hovers around 10 to 20 segments. The same 5 MB now takes 282 rounds and 23 s, about 1.7 Mbit/s.

A small window can lose the ability to detect loss quickly: with cwnd 5 and 2 segments lost, only 3 arrive, too few to generate 3 duplicate ACKs (or the tail of the transfer is lost). The sender has to wait for the retransmission timer (at least 200 ms; 240 ms at this RTT) and then restarts from cwnd 1 in slow start.

A BBR-like sender does not treat loss as the signal. It measures the delivery rate (about 100 Mbit/s) and the minimum RTT (80 ms), and keeps about one BDP (684 segments) in flight, so 1% random loss costs only retransmissions: the transfer finishes in about 0.9 s, versus 23 s for Reno.
